column1: # admin-panel/prisma/roles/grants.tsv — the admins slice of the WS-75 column grants
# Columns: role <TAB> table <TAB> privilege <TAB> columns <TAB> sequence
#   privilege  SELECT | UPDATE | INSERT | DELETE
#   columns    comma-separated, no spaces. `-` means the whole table, which only DELETE may use:
#              PostgreSQL has no column list for DELETE, and no other verb is granted table-wide
#              here (a table-level UPDATE would hand the role every column, including
#              `authentication`, which is exactly what this slice exists to prevent).
#   sequence   the sequence an INSERT must also be allowed to advance, or `-`. Its own column
#              because it is the one privilege the grant on the table does not imply: PostgreSQL
#              checks nextval() against the sequence, so INSERT alone fails on `admins` with
#              "permission denied for sequence admins_id_seq" — an error that names a different
#              object than the one an operator is looking at. Written out rather than derived from
#              the table name, so the file lists every object a role gains a privilege on.
# WHY the RLS policies are derived and not listed: the rehearsal matrix (cms-ops pentest run
# 2026-11-21, Result 4) showed the two are one rule, not two. A role with a grant and no policy
# reads zero rows, which looks like a missing record rather than a permission error — so a grant
# row emits its own policy row for the same verb, and the two can never drift. A writer also needs
# SELECT, both because `UPDATE ... WHERE` looks the row up and because Prisma writes with
# INSERT ... RETURNING; the write roles below therefore carry an explicit SELECT row.
# WHY only `admins` is listed: this step is the foundation of the split, and `admins` is the table
# whose matrix was actually exercised against a database. The other domains follow in their own
# slices, where their columns are proven the same way.
